tip: 'Barusan' = spoken 'just now'; in writing use 'baru saja': 'barusan dia telepon' = he just called.
'Mendengar' = hear (it reaches your ears); 'mendengarkan' = listen (on purpose).
'Sebelumnya' after a time word = the ... before: 'malam sebelumnya' = the night before.
'Sempat' = at some point managed/happened to: 'sempat ragu' = did hesitate for a while.
'Baru' after a time link = only then: 'sesudahnya baru kita makan' = only after that do we eat.
'Sebelumnya' can open politely: 'sebelumnya saya minta maaf...' = first of all, I apologize...
'Ketika' = when, common in writing; in everyday speech people usually say 'waktu': 'waktu saya kuliah'.
'Para' + people-noun = plural group: 'para penumpang' = the passengers.
'Membacakan' = read out for someone: 'membacakan cerita' = read a story aloud (for them).
'Sambil' = while (same person doing both): 'menyapu halaman sambil menunggu' = sweep the yard while waiting.
'Baru' + adjective = freshly/just became: 'baru kering' = just dried.
'Pas' = colloquial 'right when': 'pas saya keluar' = right as I left. Written form: 'ketika'/'waktu'.
'Sedang' + doubled adjective + '-nya' = at its peak: 'sedang seru-serunya' = at its most exciting.
Once 'antre' (queue up) takes '-an' it's a full noun: 'antrean panjang itu' – it takes an adjective, takes 'itu', and stands as the subject of the sentence.
'Awalnya ... akhirnya' frames a story: 'awalnya susah, akhirnya terbiasa' = hard at first, used to it in the end.
'Juga' after a verb can mean after all/finally: 'ikut juga' = ended up joining after all.
'Malah' = contrary to expectation: 'saya malah suka' = I actually ended up liking it.
Doubling a verb often makes it aimless and unhurried: 'melihat' = look at, 'melihat-lihat' = browse with no target. 'Hanya mau melihat-lihat' = just looking, the shop answer.
'Dulu' at the start = used to: 'dulu saya tinggal di Medan' = I used to live in Medan.
'Dulu ... sekarang' contrasts past and present: 'dulu sepi, sekarang ramai' = used to be quiet, now busy.
'Berjualan' is selling as your trade, not one transaction: 'nenek dulu berjualan kue' = grandma used to sell cakes for a living. To sell one specific thing, use 'menjual'.
'Kesiangan' = too late in the morning: 'bangun kesiangan' = overslept.
Double a time word and it stretches into a process: 'lama' = a long while, 'lama-lama' = over time, bit by bit. 'Lama-lama dia belajar memasak' = over time she learned to cook.
'Yang' after the doer = the one who: 'saya yang membuka pintu' = I'm the one who opened the door.
'Salah' + verb = do wrongly: 'salah naik bus' = take the wrong bus.
'Pakai' adds toppings when ordering: 'pakai telur' = with an egg.
'Gurih' is the savory richness of coconut milk, broth, and fried things – a core taste word English has no exact match for: 'bumbu kacang yang gurih' = savory peanut sauce.
'Kenyal' is the prized springy-bouncy bite: 'baksonya kenyal' is a compliment. The opposite, 'lembek' (mushy), is a failed 'bakso'.
'Kecap' is soy sauce, not ketchup – 'kecap manis' is the sweet, syrupy kind brushed on grilled chicken. English actually borrowed 'ketchup' from this Malay word.
'Sate' is counted in 'tusuk' (skewers): 'sepuluh tusuk' = ten skewers.
